articles.title: Ram Temple donations 'theft' case: SIT to file first chargesheet on or before September 25
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court-appointed Special Investigation Team (SIT) probing the alleged theft of donations at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya will file .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court-appointed Special Investigation Team (SIT) probing the alleged theft of donations at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya will file its first chargesheet in the case on or before September 25, a CJI-led bench was informed on Monday.Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the bench that the chargesheet would have to be filed as the statutory 90-day period from the first arrest in the case would lapse soon.“Ninety days from the date of the first arrest are going to be over on September 25, so we will have to file the chargesheet, otherwise, they (the accused) will get default bail,” Mehta said.The bench, comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, also perused a detailed status report submitted by the SIT in a sealed cover.Under Section 167(2) of the CrPC, an accused becomes entitled to statutory bail if the investigating agency fails to file a chargesheet in the trial court within the stipulated period of 60 or 90 days.The bench had earlier directed the probe team to complete its investigation expeditiously and take it to its logical conclusion. It had also asked the SIT to file a status report in a sealed cover on the progress of the probe into the alleged theft of donations.The Supreme court had taken note of the formation of a four-member SIT headed by IGP Kiran S to investigate the alleged embezzlement of donations and directed the Uttar Pradesh government to include a forensic auditor in the probe team.Observing that “remedial actions will have to be taken”, the bench had said steps would be taken to “ensure transparency” and directed the SIT to submit a status report.The court's directions came after allegations of irregularities surfaced in the management of donations at the Ram Temple. Several petitioners approached the Supreme Court seeking a CBI probe and a forensic audit of the temple trust’s finances.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac buy Wrexham pub The Turf
articles.summary: The Turf is a regular feature on the Welcome to Wrexham Disney documentary series.
articles.body:
Wrexham's Hollywood co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have bought the pub next door to the football club's Racecourse home ground to "protect the future of the club".

Wrexham AFC was founded at the then-named Turf Hotel in October 1864 and is the oldest football club in Wales.

A club statement announcing the purchase from Admiral Taverns said it hoped to "help protect the historic pub" by "incorporating the club, the Racecourse Ground and The Turf under a single ownership".

The pub and its landlord, Wayne Jones, have become regular features on the award-winning "Welcome to Wrexham" Disney documentary series, and Jones described the buy as "great news for all Wrexham fans".

Celebrities have been spotted visiting The Turf since Reynolds and Mac took over the club in 2021, including Paul Rudd , Channing Tatum and Will Ferrell .

The club statement continued: "The acquisition allows for the preservation of the history and traditions of the historic public house that is inexorably linked to the Racecourse Ground and Wrexham AFC Football Club since its foundation in 1864.

"This will include opportunities to enhance the current fan zone and other fan-related activities in the area next to The Turf on the Mold Road.

"The acquisition of The Turf is a continuation of the strategy to protect the future of the club and its interests by ring fencing key areas related to the life of the club."

"The Turf Tavern, as it was then, predates the club and records suggest that the club itself was founded in the pub," said Jones, who has been landlord of The Turf for the past 20 years."

"It has played a key part of the club's history ever since, with the players changing in the pub before running out onto the Racecourse Ground as recently as the 1940s.

"It continues to be a focal point for fans on matchdays and non-matchdays," Jones added.

Jones will continue running the pub as part of the purchase deal, and said he was looking forward to bringing its "unique mix of history, atmosphere and sometimes Hollywood stardust" to the next generation of Wrexham fans and locals alike.

The Racecourse Ground staged its first Wales fixture in March 1877 and is the world's oldest football stadium still hosting international matches.

Eric Allyn, on behalf of minority investors the Allyn family, said: "Ever since we invested in Wrexham AFC through Red Dragon Ventures in 2024, the town, the community and the football club have become a second home.

"By bringing The Turf into the group, we are securing the long-term future of the pub and with it preserving its history and that of the club."

articles.title: In 2018, Jon Bon Jovi paid $10 million for a Palm Beach home, demolished it and rebuilt; two years later he sold the new mansion for $19.85 million and bought a $43 million estate
articles.summary: Real Estate News: Rock star Jon Bon Jovi made a quick multi-million-pound property deal in South Florida, selling a newly built oceanfront mansion in Palm Beach for $19.
articles.body: Rock star Jon Bon Jovi made a quick multi-million-pound property deal in South Florida, selling a newly built oceanfront mansion in Palm Beach for $19.85 million (£15.8 million), just two years after buying the original property for about half that amount. According to property records and local real estate reports, first detailed by The Real Deal, the musician completed the sale of the custom-built home on North Ocean Boulevard in July 2020. On the same day, he bought a much larger oceanfront estate farther south on South Ocean Boulevard for $43 million (£34.2 million). The two deals represent one of the fastest and most profitable residential redevelopments by a celebrity in Palm Beach in recent years.A $10 million property makeoverBon Jovi bought the original property at 1075 North Ocean Boulevard in 2018 through a limited liability company for $10 million. Instead of moving into the existing 1950s house, the singer decided to demolish it. He then built a custom two-storey mansion covering about 5,000 square feet. The home was designed in a modern Mediterranean style. The finished property has five bedrooms, five full bathrooms and two half-bathrooms. It also includes an oceanfront swimming pool, a covered loggia, a courtyard, an elevator and a two-car garage. Yahoo News reported that the property was initially listed for $22.9 million before the asking price was reduced. The final sale price of $19.85 million gave Bon Jovi a large gross gain compared with the original $10 million land purchase, although construction costs would have reduced the overall profit.Moving to a larger estateInstead of keeping the property or using the proceeds elsewhere, Jon Bon Jovi immediately put the money into a much larger Palm Beach estate. Records show that he bought 1020 South Ocean Boulevard on the same day the North Ocean Boulevard property was sold. The seller was a company linked to real estate developer and trial attorney Thomas Holofcener. The new estate sits on more than one acre of land and has much more living space. The mansion covers more than 10,000 square feet and includes seven bedrooms, seven full bathrooms and five half-bathrooms. Built in 2007, the home has several luxury features, including a courtyard, swimming pool, wine cellar, full home gym and a separate apartment for staff. It also has direct beach access across the street, making it especially attractive in Palm Beach’s luxury property market.Palm Beach’s property boomThe two transactions also show how strong South Florida’s luxury property market was in 2020. Wealthy buyers, especially from New York and New Jersey, increasingly looked to Florida for primary and second homes because of its tax advantages and warm climate. Palm Beach was one of the areas that saw strong sales and rising property prices during 2020. High-end buyers were purchasing land, renovating older homes and tearing down existing properties to build new custom oceanfront estates. Jon Bon Jovi is one of several well-known public figures who have invested in property in the area, joining other wealthy homeowners in the exclusive beachfront community. The buyer of Bon Jovi’s North Ocean Boulevard home was not publicly identified in property records. The sale was completed through a trustee account.Holdouts against mega-assemblagesIn mid-2025, reports from Realtor.com and The Wall Street Journal said that Bon Jovi’s $43 million estate on South Ocean Boulevard had become a key target in a major land-buying effort. A mystery buyer, reportedly linked to tech billionaires, spent more than $250 million buying nearby properties. This included an adjacent 2.8-acre oceanfront plot bought from cosmetics heir William Lauder for about $178 million. According to industry reports, Bon Jovi repeatedly turned down multi-million-dollar offers to sell his property. He chose to keep his 10,000-square-foot estate despite strong pressure to sell as buyers continued assembling large amounts of land in the area.Billionaires’ Row expansionsKen Griffin (Citadel): The hedge fund founder has acquired more than 27 connected acres along South County Road in Palm Beach. He has spent well over $350 million on several mansions and oceanfront properties, including the historic $105 million La Follia estate. His purchases are intended to create one of the largest private residential compounds in U.S. history.William Lauder: The Estée Lauder heir spent more than $25 million in 2020 buying neighboring properties on North Ocean Boulevard. He demolished the existing homes and later offered the combined property for between $178 million and $200 million.Broader South Florida celebrity relocationsBilly Joel: In late 2024, the musician completed the sale of his large oceanfront estate in Manalapan for $42.6 million. He later bought a $40 million waterfront home in Boca Raton’s Sanctuary community.Mark Wahlberg: After selling his $63 million Beverly Hills mansion, Wahlberg bought a $37 million estate at Stone Creek Ranch in Delray Beach.Kevin James: The actor purchased a $17.15 million custom-built home in Boca Raton’s Royal Palm Yacht & Country Club. His move reflects the growing interest among high-profile buyers in private, gated communities across South Florida.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Bessent on talks with China ahead of Trump-Xi meeting: ‘Very successful engagement’
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday said recent talks with Chinese officials went well, a few days before President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet later this week. “We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI, completing where we left off in Beijing. We created…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday said recent talks with Chinese officials went well, a few days before President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet later this week.

“We just had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI, completing where we left off in Beijing. We created the board of trade and began the subject of AI, and this evening, those were operationalized,” the Treasury secretary said Sunday in New York City.

On Wednesday, Trump is set to greet Xi when the Chinese leader arrives at Joint Base Andrews. The Chinese president’s arrival will begin a state visit to the White House, featuring bilateral meetings and a state dinner.

Xi’s upcoming trip follows Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May. Trump has praised the Chinese president in spite of U.S.-Chinese tensions, calling him a “great leader” and a “strong man.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who was with Bessent in New York on Sunday, has proposed a “board of trade” as a forum for U.S. officials and their Chinese counterparts to figure out what goods the two countries can sustainably trade with each other, versus products under the category of sensitive technology that raise security problems.

Warnings about the dangers of unlimited AI are placing additional urgency on Trump and Xi’s upcoming talks . Trump has waved away AI’s existential threats as a “hoax,” an outlook aligned with Beijing’s general view, according to analysts. Heated competition to lead on the technology and mutual distrust have delayed discussions between the U.S. and China on AI safeguards and regulations.

articles.title: Friedrich Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
articles.summary: Political shifts in Germany are being watched closely in Europe and beyond, Katya Adler writes.
articles.body:
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker.

The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them.

The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield.

At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began.

German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems.

He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks.

The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament .

Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well.

It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist.

The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past.

The party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want.

Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party.

The AfD accuses Merz of failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets.

High time for political change, says the AfD.

Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician.

Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party.

I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual.

Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted.

Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed.

He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required.

Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future.

Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped.

Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people.

Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology.

In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive".

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect.

Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy.

Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget.

When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable.

Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example.

This comes at a time when the EU wants to spend more, not less, on common defence projects, migration and AI and tech.

Faced with perceived threats from Russia and China, wars in the Middle East affecting energy supplies and prices, plus the unpredictability - and many in Europe say, unreliability - of the US under Trump, now is a time Europeans must stick tightly together, says Brussels.

The EU is watching Merz's travails, plus the strengthening of the AfD on the right and the hard left Die Linke too, with concern.

These regional German votes come at the start of bumper election season across the EU, where all the big powers - (including France, Italy, Spain and Poland - go to the polls.

Nationalist, Eurosceptic, anti-immigration parties are predicted to do well. And Beijing and Moscow are watching closely.

articles.title: Merz vows to keep ruling coalition together for sake of Germany's 'democratic future'
articles.summary: The chancellor has come under increasing pressure after resounding state election defeats, but says the results "go far beyond my own person"
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he will keep his ruling coalition together for the sake of his country's "democratic future", following resounding defeats for his party in two state elections.

"We are determined to live up to the historic challenges our country is facing," Merz said, referring to the coalition between his Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

Merz's position has come under mounting pressure after Sunday's election results. In the north-eastern Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the most votes, with the CDU failing even to reach the threshold to stay in the state parliament.

Meanwhile in Berlin, the CDU came second to the hard-left Die Linke party, with the AfD also making significant gains.

Katya Adler: Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability

Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow" for the centre-right CDU.

"This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic, unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany," he acknowledged.

Merz said there had been no discussion about his own position since the results and pushed back against the idea that his low popularity ratings alone were behind the election defeats.

"I know that I as an individual played a role in these state elections," Merz said, before adding: "But the reasons for the results go far beyond just me."

"We are witnessing a profound transformation of Germany's political party system, as is happening in many other countries around the world."

There have been rumours Merz, who has only been in power for 16 months, could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap due to his poor approval ratings.

Asked earlier on Monday how long Merz has left in office, the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel told the BBC: "Pretty soon, he's going to leave."

The two elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory.

In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU fell short of a 5% threshold to enter parliament, underperforming against what had already been projected to be the party's worst ever result in the area. Merz earlier conceded that this result was "a disaster".

While the AfD won the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, it was far short of a majority and is unlikely to govern as other parties may refuse to work with it.

Some branches of the party are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.

But its anti-immigration, Germany first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.

In Berlin, the CDU's defeat means Die Linke, which won the most votes, could now take power in a coalition.

Elif Eralp, who led the party to victory in the capital, promised to tackle unaffordable rent prices in remarks made after the results came out.

"The people of Berlin have clearly opted for a change in policy, specifically for an affordable Berlin, for policies that solve the rent crisis and put people first," she told German news outlet The Pioneer.

During the election campaign, Eralp pledged to expropriate more than 200,000 housing units from private landlords. Merz has promised to pursue legislation to prevent such actions, citing the impact on foreign investment.

articles.title: Endangered Black Robin aka 'Karure' named New Zealand's 2026 Bird of the Year
articles.summary: Rest of World News: New Zealand's critically endangered black robin, the karure, has been crowned Bird of the Year 2026 after receiving a record 25,000 votes. With a population of around 350, conservationists aim to establish a third population to ensure the species' survival. Find out more about the Bird of the Year contest and its significance.
articles.body: New Zealand's critically endangered black robin, known as the “karure”, has been named the country's 2026 Bird of the Year after securing more than 25,000 votes in a record-breaking public contest.The small black bird, found only on the remote Chatham Islands about 800 kilometres east of mainland New Zealand, finished ahead of the kākāpō and the New Zealand falcon, which placed second and third respectively.More than 105,000 people voted in this year's competition, according to conservation group Forest & Bird. That was the highest turnout since the contest began, with about 88% of the votes coming from within New Zealand.From five birds to around 350The karure's victory comes as its population continues to recover from a near-extinction crisis.By 1980, only five black robins remained. Just one of them, a female known as Old Blue, was capable of breeding. Conservationists began a recovery programme using Old Blue and a male called Old Yellow as the founding pair, according to Forest & Bird as cited by CNN.There are now about 350 adult black robins living on two pest-free reserve islands.The recovery made the species a prominent example of New Zealand's conservation efforts, but its future remains uncertain. The Department of Conservation classifies the karure as Threatened-Nationally Critical, while conservationists say the existing habitat is close to capacity.They want to establish another population on a third island to allow the species to continue growing.Record turnout for Bird of the YearThe 2026 vote attracted more than 105,000 ballots, up from more than 75,000 in 2025. The figure is a significant increase from the competition's first edition two decades ago, when fewer than 900 votes were recorded.This year's contest used an election-style format, with birds grouped into parties including Shy Birds, Floor Birds, Night Birds and High Birds.Conservation message behind the contestForest & Bird said the competition is intended to draw attention to native wildlife and the threats facing endangered species.Rebecca Hatch, the group's manager for growing support, said the humour surrounding the contest helped draw attention to a more serious conservation issue."The jokes are funny and this year's meme game certainly didn't disappoint, but underneath it all there is a serious message," Hatch said.Forest & Bird says 80% of New Zealand's native bird species are facing some level of trouble or serious threat.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: London designers want to remind you that humans made these clothes
articles.summary: In an increasingly automated world, some brands went to great lengths to emphasize the human engine behind fashion week.
articles.body: This season, many of the designers showing at London Fashion Week seemed to want to remind us of one thing: humans made these clothes. It was an idea placed front and center at the Steve O Smith show — which wasn’t a show at all, but a seminar, delivered by Smith himself to 20 or so fashion editors and journalists in a cozy drawing room at the Royal Academy of Arts. Each look was carefully broken down not just in terms of narrative but also granular technique — a luxury compared to the three second fly-by of typical runway shows — from the appliqué sewn on tulle to beading embellishment, panniers and ties cut out of shirts. At the end of the masterclass, Smith gushed effusively of his “incredibly small team” from behind the lecture stand. “It makes me a little bit emotional,” he said. “There’s one seamstress, Joanna, who made everything you’ve seen today. We have one beading artist, Saskia, and Thomas, who is my assistant designer, who is absolutely incredible.” Backstage at Pauline Dujancourt’s fourth London runway show, the designer — who is part of the prestigious Paul Smith’s Foundation fashion residency program — spoke at length about the 700 hand-crocheted flowers used to adorn one of her ethereal gowns. Each bloom of yarn took between 10 and 15 minutes to make, she said, and many were constructed in Peru by women Dujancourt was able to employ with the money from her Andam Prize win earlier this summer. Her clients in particular love “to know how long it took to make something,” she said. At Labrum, before guests even saw the clothes on the runway, they got to meet the hands that helped make them. By the doorway to the catwalk two people sat toiling at desks, one hand-beading a piece of cloth and the other machine sewing a denim garment. It was a “performance piece,” they said, though both were actually part of Labrum’s design team. The collection featured hand-woven raffia trousers made in India, as well as shirts, shorts and skirts hand-embroidered with scenes from Sierra Leone. “People don’t understand how things are made and where they’re from,” founder Foday Dumbuya said after the show. “That’s why we wanted to put it at the forefront and celebrate it.” Currently it’s taken for granted that some person, either with a needle or a sewing machine, made what you are wearing — whether they were paid fairly or worked in safe conditions is less certain. But who knows how much longer that human touch will be guaranteed. AI, which has steadily infiltrated design workflows over the last few years, is now being developed by robotics companies to take on more physical tasks like pattern cutting, sewing and quality inspection in countries like South Korea. When asked whether he thought about AI’s impact on the fashion industry, Dumbuya replied “100%.” “I don’t buy AI,” he continued. “The moment we kill that human interaction, we’re gone.” Talia Loubaton, founder and designer at Liberowe, went a step further than simply talking about her method. On Sunday afternoon she folded journalists, editors, buyers and even some of her customers right into it by using the presentation to shoot her campaign imagery. The backstage of a runway is usually a hectic underside designers would rather pull a curtain around, but here it was all hanging out. “I think it’s interesting to make it quite immersive,” Loubaton said, as busy stylists and photographers zipped around her, slamming sticky-notes on the giant model board to indicate when they’d photographed a look. She spoke of the importance of “being in the same room and being able to talk through the collection, meet and speak with each other and show you how we work, how we create the imagery and get you in the process.” This emphasis on the human collateral of fashion week — design teams, photographers, stylists, seamstresses — felt like the real display of luxury. Perhaps it was a deliberate act of technological resistance by designers, or perhaps the old analog ways of working feel new and poignant in our AI-driven world. One thing was for sure: none of these hands were idle.

images.caption: LONDON, ENGLAND - SEPTEMBER 19: Models backstage before the Steve O Smith show during London Fashion Week September 2026 at Royal Academy of Arts on September 19, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Tristan Fewings/Getty Images)
Smith ran a tight group through the technique and artistry of his new collection.
His fabric appliqué designs had gauzy backing and beaded embellishments.
The waifish finale look at Pauline Dujancourt’s show featured 700 hand-crocheted flowers, while the runway had 4,000 handmade flowers.
“This collection is about celebrating the people behind the cloth,” Foday Dumbuya said backstage at the Labrum show.
Many elements of the collection were hand-completed, from the raffia trousers to the embroidery of tropical scenes stitched into skirts, shorts and shirts.
Patrick McDowell was inspired by the colors and textures of Wong Kar-wai's 2000 film, "In the Mood for Love."
Backstage, Simone Rocha said that she "didn’t want to get too bogged down in narrative” this season. Instead wanted to focus on “purity” and “effortlessness.”
The exposed under garments, lack of embellishments and stripped-back styling was a new direction for Rocha.
“Sometimes I can be very layered, and I can really like put clothes on top of clothes. It's a very protective thing," Rocha said.

articles.title: Elif Eralp: A leftist leader with Turkish roots dubbed ‘Germany’s Mamdani’
articles.summary: Victory in Berlin signals that Germany continues to be liberal, that, despite the far right’s rise, experts say.
articles.body:
When Elif Eralp was 10, she rallied her friends to make hand-painted posters in her family’s garage, calling for the protection of the environment.

It was the early nineties in Germany and this was one of her first forays into activism. Her parents also inspired her by taking her along to political demonstrations.

Now, 35 years later, Eralp is taking her social justice advocacy to new heights.

On Sunday, her The Left party (Die Linke) won first place in Berlin’s state election – putting her on course to potentially become the next governing mayor of Germany’s gritty, creative capital.

Born in Munich to Turkish socialists and trade unionists who fled the 1980 military coup in Turkiye, Eralp’s victory could mark several firsts. She would be the first The Left party candidate to lead Berlin since German reunification in 1990, the city’s first mayor of Turkish descent – and its first woman of colour to hold the office.

Victory signals ‘strong desire for disruption’

Eralp’s campaign promises of affordable housing, rent controls and more political inclusion for immigrants and refugees contrasted with her rivals, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Two weeks ago, the AfD triumphed in Saxony-Anhalt . But on Sunday, they came third in Berlin.

Eralp’s party nabbed the most votes, but it now needs allies to take control of the mayor’s office.

As Germans look beyond traditional political candidates, her appeal may have grown, experts say.

“There was a strong desire for disruption and radical political change,” Martin Fuchs, a German political and digital consultant, told Al Jazeera.

Additionally, Eralp’s win after the AfD’s “shows that, in 2026, Germany is not only witnessing a rise in far-right parties, but [that] there continues to be a colourful, diverse, open and liberal Germany,” he added.

A member of The Left party since 2017, she wants to see “alternatives to neoliberal policies” and seeks to confront the “racist AfD”, according to her website.

“Without an active civil society, progress to the left cannot be achieved,” she said.

She has served in the Berlin House of Representatives since 2021 and became deputy chair of The Left party’s parliamentary group in 2024.

She had a lengthy legal career, having studied law in Hamburg and worked for more than a decade as a legal adviser for The Left.

The daughter of refugees has long advocated for migrant rights.

Eralp interned with the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, cofounded a migrant rights network within The Left party and is pushing for Berlin to become a “solidarity city”.

That designation would see the German capital become more welcoming to refugees, end “stigmatising police checks”, she said, and improve immigrants’ participation in civil society.

She campaigned on a nationwide rent cap and wants more housing placed under municipal ownership.

“I stand for a social policy – a policy that brings everyone along. And the priority now is making Berlin affordable,” she said in her victory speech on Sunday.

Edward Goodger, a lecturer in politics at the University of Manchester studying the left and populism, said Die Linke has now edged out other leftists, such as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance.

“An Eralp-led government could provide another prominent political (force) who could act as a rallying point for radical-left politics in Germany,” Goodger told Al Jazeera.

Beyond rent freezes, Eralp has loftier goals as mayor, such as hosting a New Year reception for the homeless at city hall.

She embraced the New York mayor’s democratic socialist message as a campaign blueprint, with some calling her “Germany’s Mamdani ”.

Some of her party members travelled to New York to learn more about Zohran Mamdani’s campaign and meet with his advisers.

Eralp said his victory last year offered a model for left-wing parties worldwide, including in Germany. Both focused on fighting social injustice and making major cities more affordable.

Her online presence was also crucial to her success, said Fuchs.

“With the help of highly professional ‘vibe’ content – modelled on Zohran Mamdani’s campaign in New York … [she] managed to connect with the everyday realities of many Berliners,” he said.

Translation: Zohran Mamdani shows that a different kind of politics is possible. A victory for the working class – achieved through an inspiring campaign and policies that improve people’s lives. What lessons can we draw from this for Berlin? Join us as we discuss strategies, successes, and next steps with Elif Eralp, Maximilian Schirmer, Franziska Heinisch and Liza Pflaum. Come along and join the conversation!

Eralp was by far the most visible candidate on social media, amassing the highest number of views across platforms at 6.3 million, according to an analytics platform, viral.app.

“Eralp’s election could serve as a significant symbol, encouraging even more people from migrant communities to get involved in politics and to feel seen and heard in this society,” Fuchs said. “[It] could strengthen cohesion between citizens with and without a migrant background and thus help to counter division.”

Gero Neugebauer, a professor of political science at The Free University of Berlin, said Eralp is well suited to lead a German city, home to many immigrant communities since the 1960s.

“Eralp has Turkish parents, was born in Munich and holds both German and Turkish citizenship. In this respect, [her taking] office would confirm the slogan: ‘Look, this is Berlin’,” Neugebauer told Al Jazeera, referring to the local cultural catchphrase.

But The Left party must still secure coalition partners and a majority in Berlin’s House of Representatives, which elects the governing mayor.

While in office, Eralp could struggle to fulfil some of her election promises, said Fuchs.

She will have to convince about half of Berliners – which includes the business community – about her housing reforms, which could also involve lengthy legal hurdles, he said.

That legal battle could play out as a potential conflict between the federal government and the state government, said Neugebauer.

The Left party has also faced accusations of anti-Semitism – and would need to distance itself from them, Fuchs explained.

But Eralp’s win has made one thing imminently clear: Germans are looking for alternatives.

“The result from Berlin seems to be following a much wider trend currently being seen in German politics: Voters looking beyond the established mainstream parties, with this dissatisfaction being channelled to both radical-left and radical-right challenger parties,” said Goodger.

articles.title: Americans warned again to rethink travel as missile attack rattles historic region
articles.summary: A Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh over the weekend prompted the State Department to renew warnings to Americans of potential flight cancellations and airspace closures in key areas.
articles.body: The State Department renewed its warning on Saturday to Americans who may be traveling in and through the Middle East as escalating regional tensions raise concerns among travelers. The warning came as Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched a ballistic missile toward Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, over the weekend — which Saudi Arabia said its air defenses intercepted. Residents reported hearing an explosion and later seeing a plume of smoke near King Khalid International Airport, according to The Associated Press (AP). No casualties or damage from the attack were reported. AMERICANS WARNED AGAINST TRAVEL PLANS AS TERRORISM THREATENS POPULAR DESTINATION In an X post on Saturday, the State Department's Bureau of Consular Affairs warned that the security environment in the Middle East "remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation." The agency added, "Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions." Officials specifically cited hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in its warning. "Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports," the post said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly. Americans outside the Middle East should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region." The agency also advised those traveling to or from the region to monitor airport and airline operations, warning that U.S. diplomatic facilities have been targeted, including outside the Middle East. "Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U.S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including U.S. businesses and other institutions," the post added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The alert comes as a periodic reminder from the State Department and does not signal a change in advisory status. The worldwide caution has been in place since February. The latest warning follows a series of similar alerts from U.S. officials amid heightened tensions across the region. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In June, U.S. officials similarly urged Americans across the Middle East to remain vigilant as tensions mounted across the region. At the time, officials warned that airspace closures, demonstrations and threats to locations associated with the United States could disrupt travel with little notice. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The State Department also maintained its "Level 3: Reconsider Travel" advisory for Oman in an Aug. 30 update, warning of risks from armed conflict and terrorism, including the threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran. The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title: Scotland's 32 councils could be cut to six under government plan
articles.summary: Reforms could involve the creation of six to 10 regional authorities, as well as more than 100 community bodies.
articles.body:
Scotland's 32 councils could be replaced by as few as six regional authorities, the government has suggested.

Under proposals for a new two-tier system, the regional bodies would focus on major issues such as education and economic growth.

Between 120 and 160 community authorities would also be created. They would be expected to contribute to local issues such as licensing and town centre improvements.

The reforms have been shared with Holyrood's committees and council umbrella body Cosla ahead of a public consultation.

Scotland's councils face budget shortfalls. How bad is it in your area?

How will Swinney 'rewire' local government and public services?

The proposals suggest that the regional bodies would be given powers over larger planning decisions, education and economic development.

They would also oversee the delivery of key services such as waste management, cleaning and early learning.

The smaller community authorities would contribute to areas including local planning decisions, town centre regeneration, licensing and the historic environment.

Separate set-ups for Scotland's islands would also be required, according to the paper.

Councillors would be elected to the existing wards across Scotland and serve on both the local and regional authorities.

However, the document suggests the increased time commitment may require a boost in pay.

The proposals do not outline how the reforms would be financed.

Scotland's current council set-up, with 32 local authorities, was introduced by the UK government in 1996.

Before then, the country had a two-tier system of nine regional councils and 53 district councils.

Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth described the proposals as a "starting point" for reform.

"We need to ensure investment is focused on frontline delivery, with the right staff in the right roles to empower communities and deliver real improvements in public services," she added.

"Existing local government responsibilities could also be extended, including enhanced roles in economic development and business support so that individual areas can reflect local strengths and ambitions."

STUC General Secretary Roz Foyer said: "Whilst the Scottish government have the laudable ambition to strengthen local democracy, it's absolutely for the birds to think the sheer scale of this local government reform can be achieved without the initial and substantial investment required to bring about change in our communities.

"There is an argument that community authorities can improve decision making but only if the funding exists to deliver these services.

"The Scottish government must be clear that, in the short-term, this will cost money - not save it."

Scottish Labour local government spokesman Joe Fagan said: "The Scottish government must not blunder into another reorganisation.

"Any reforms must be made in partnership with local government and backed up with fair funding for local services."

Conservative spokesman Alexander Burnett MSP described the proposals as "half-baked", while LibDem MSP Morven-May MacCallum called for the government to set out evidence that the reforms could "lift Scottish education back up the international rankings, speed up planning, fix the potholes or ease the financial strain on local services".

The proposed reforms come as the government aims to cut public spending and improve efficiency.

Earlier this month, First Minister John Swinney announced plans to reduce the number of health boards in Scotland from 14 to two.

He described the reforms as "the most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era".

Analysis: Bold plans, with limited detail

This is bigger and bolder than anything ministers have previously described.

It's presented as an outline for discussion rather than a pre-determined outcome. If implemented, it would be the most extensive shake-up of local government for 30 years.

When the SNP manifesto referred to reducing the number of public bodies, it was not explicit about councils. The first minister made clear that he wanted fewer of them in a Holyrood statement earlier this month.

He has since met council leaders who asked him to spell out his vision and that's what we now have, with very limited detail.

The proposal is for a system of regional government whose councillors would also serve on "community authorities" that would make some decisions at a much more local level.

Ministers say they want to agree changes with local government and others within a few months - that's lightning speed for reforms of this sort.

Council leaders will meet for further discussions on Friday having previously expressed concern about potentially losing control of social care provision to the NHS.

articles.title: As US steers clear of Yemen fight, the Iran-backed Houthis launch next phase of campaign
articles.summary: In the last month, Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen have joined the Middle East conflict in dramatic fashion – capturing a swathe of the Red Sea coastline, sending missiles and drones against Saudi energy infrastructure and even targeting the Saudi capital Riyadh on the weekend.
articles.body: In the last month, Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen have joined the Middle East conflict in dramatic fashion – capturing a swathe of the Red Sea coastline, sending missiles and drones against Saudi energy infrastructure and even targeting the Saudi capital Riyadh on the weekend. Now their campaign appears to be entering a new phase, with a major offensive aimed at cutting off government forces in a central part of Yemen. Their ultimate goal – according to some analysts – is control of the entire country. The latest Houthi advance comes as Saudi Arabia deploys fighter jets and missiles in an effort to stem the militant group’s progress south towards the port city of Aden, where Yemen’s internationally-recognized government is based. Saudi appeals for US airstrikes to reverse Houthi gains have fallen on deaf ears, according to a regional diplomatic source. The Houthis have already seized a long stretch of the Yemeni coastline adjacent to the Red Sea – one of the world’s most important waterways – and control the Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint at its southern end. Now, they are trying to take control of the mountainous region of Taiz, which includes important routes for government forces. “Cutting these routes would threaten a key transport and supply connection between government-held areas,” according to Yemen analyst Mohammed al-Basha. The Houthis have run into stiff resistance from local tribes, Basha told CNN. The battlefield situation remains fluid, according to Basha, and the risk remains that the Houthis will be able to surround the city of Taiz. But it appears that defenses have not experienced a collapse comparable to what was seen on the west coast front, when a large area – including the port of Mocha – fell within hours. Basha added that, as of Monday, a critical road junction connecting Taiz and Aden in an area hosting hundreds of thousands of internally-displaced people remains in government hands. There is also heavy fighting further east, according to several Yemen analysts, in the province of Marib near the border with Saudi Arabia. Marib is an oil-rich region long in the Houthis’ sights. Yemeni government forces have used artillery and rocket systems – supported by Saudi airstrikes of growing intensity – to repel Houthi forces in the region, according to analysts, and a senior commander claimed that his troops had now gone on the offensive. “The Houthis likely seek to capture the area in order to try to extract and export oil through the Red Sea, which could fund Houthi political and military activities,” according to the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington think-tank, on Friday. “Taiz and Marib cities are the bastions of north Yemen and if the Houthis capture both it is game over – but their defenders are putting up a strong fight,” Basha told CNN. It’s unclear whether the Houthis intend to put pressure on Aden itself. Much will depend on the ability of government forces to improve coordination after the disastrous western shore retreat. “The Houthis do not need to defeat Saudi Arabia militarily and near certainly cannot,” says Ibrahim Jalal of the Middle East Institute in Washington. “They, however, need to influence how much financing, intelligence, logistics, air defence and potentially airpower Riyadh is prepared to commit to the Yemeni Armed Forces capable of reversing their gains on the ground.” To that end, Jalal told CNN, the Houthis are avoiding getting bogged down in urban fighting and trying to encircle government forces. CNN has contacted Houthi officials for comment. The New York Times reported Monday that, after a call from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman last week, US President Donald Trump had agreed to launch air strikes against the Houthis. But Trump changed his mind on Sunday, according to the Times. Last week, Trump said the Houthis “let us know they don’t want to fight with us,” adding that they were allowing “most ships” to pass through the Bab al Mandeb strait but were “unhappy” with one country – obviously Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said two months ago that they would attack Saudi shipping. “Trump’s best option is to stay out of the Yemen quagmire as remote warfare won’t change the equilibrium on the ground while widening supply chain disruption,” according to Andreas Krieg, CEO of London-based political risk firm MENA Analytica. “It would also derail the Iran and Hormuz diplomatic track,” Krieg wrote on X Monday. However, the “inconsistency in the US position vis-à-vis Tehran’s proxies means that the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia have had to handle the Houthis largely on their own,” Fatima Abo Alasrar, a Yemeni analyst, wrote in a piece for the Stimson Center, a US research institute. So far, Saudi Arabia does not appear to have invoked its recently agreed trilateral defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. And Turkish officials have been careful not to offer too much. “We see there are very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity, sovereignty,” Turkish Foreign Minister Hasan Fidan said on Saturday, referring to Houthi drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia. “We are in serious solidarity on this point… They may have some military needs, especially on some technical issues. We would have no issues in meeting these,” Fidan told Turkish channel NTV. Saudi isolation “Saudi Arabia is discovering how alone it is in a moment of need,” analyst Natiq Malikzada said Monday. “For years, it built its security around the hope that Washington would defend it.” “For the US, as for any other country in times like this, Saudi security matters less when American interests are not directly at risk,” Malikzada wrote on X. Jalal says the Saudis can count on some support from regional allies and Pakistan, and potentially from Egypt. But for now they bear the lion’s share of the burden. Iran is banking on the Houthis as its “last resilient proxy to improve its bargaining position and leverage, while the Houthis now seek to consolidate gains and expand territorially, as well as intensify attacks into Saudi Arabia, to redraw the rules of the game,” Jalal wrote in the online publication Al Majalla. The Houthis “will continue to punish Saudis till they get their multi-billion dollar reparations fund,” Basha told CNN Monday. They have long insisted on Saudi compensation for the long blockade against Yemeni territory they hold. But Houthi ambitions may go further. Jalal says their ultimate goal is control of all of Yemen. Javan Online, an Iranian publication affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), recently suggested the Houthis were close to unifying Yemen under a “single center of power.” In so doing they would become a regional force capable of making their opponents negotiate over Red Sea security and the future of the Arabian Peninsula itself, the Javan commentary said. That is Saudi Arabia’s nightmare. CNN’s Nadeen Ebrahim contributed reporting.

articles.title: London Fashion Week 2026: The five trends we'll see in spring
articles.summary: As London Fashion Week comes to a close, here are the biggest trends for your wardrobe.
articles.body:
This London Fashion Week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs.

The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us".

Creative director Seán McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses.

Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers.

Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth".

Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026:

"The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season.

She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quite luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year.

Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion.

She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy".

This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives.

According to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world.

A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower.

"There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats.

It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu.

Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show.

Whilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film.

Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer.

Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes".

Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics.

Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide.

"Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes.

Whether your preference is melon, tangerine, ginger or coral - orange appears to be the big colour trend for next year.

Kotsoni says she is hedging her bets on whether a shade of orange will be Pantone's colour of the year for 2027 as it has already been making its way into celebrity styling (it's not too late to replicate Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet's matching neon outfits at the Marty Supreme premiere for Halloween) and on the runway.

Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in their London shows and presentations over the last couple of days.

Ever the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet.

After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year.

Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall.

"Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel.

"Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

articles.title: Congress must repeal 1992 law hindering growth in the South Caucasus
articles.summary: As conflict escalates in the Strait of Hormuz, Rep. Anna Paulina Luna has introduced legislation to repeal a 34-year-old ban on direct U.S. aid to Azerbaijan to bolster the strategic Middle Corridor energy route.
articles.body:
American drivers are paying more at the pump because Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz into a war zone, and the safest overland alternative runs straight through a country Congress has punished by an obsolete law for 34 years.

The 1992 Freedom Support Act bars direct U.S. government assistance to Baku, a distinction no other former Soviet state carries. It was written, however, for a war that ended more than 30 years ago, in a 1994 ceasefire. The U.S. plays a whole different ballgame in the South Caucasus, a vital nexus between Europe and Central Asia, and between Russia and the Middle East, that combines energy and geostrategy.

The timing isn’t just about tidying up outdated law; this comes at a time when Iran and the U.S. are at war. China has been carefully tightening its grip on Central Asia, and Armenia and Azerbaijan, after decades of hostility, are closer to a real peace than they have been since the Soviet collapse. It is now up to Congress to back that talk of partnership with actual legislative action.

President Trump hosted Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan on Aug. 8, 2025. There, the two leaders initialed a peace framework and signed a joint declaration establishing the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity or TRIPP, a 27-mile corridor through Armenia’s Syunik province linking Azerbaijan to its Nakhichevan exclave. It was, by any measure, a genuine diplomatic breakthrough after 37 years of hostility.

Pashinyan has now won himself more room to maneuver: His Civil Contract party took 49.75 percent in Armenia’s June 2026 parliamentary vote, defeating Kremlin-backed opposition amid an active Russian disinformation campaign. Pashinyan has the public behind him, but not yet the votes. The U.S. could break the deadlock with a gesture of good faith toward Baku.

This part of the case is not theoretical; it’s happening right now. The U.S. and Iran have been entangled in conflict since Feb. 28, 2026. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which once carried roughly a fifth of the world’s traded oil remains well below normal.

That has turned Azerbaijan’s Middle Corridor, the Iran-bypassing land route linking Central Asia to Europe through the Caspian and the South Caucasus, from a hedge into a necessity. The route carried 17 million tons of freight in 2025; the Baku port is being expanded from 15 to 25 million tons of annual capacity, and the modernized Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway now runs at 5 million tons. Beijing has already bought into that same infrastructure — China Railway’s container arm joined the Azerbaijani-Georgian-Kazakh joint venture that runs the corridor last year, even as China has moved fast to fill the vacuum left by a weakened Russia across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan.

It is less a way around China than a way to keep options open: a corridor where neither Moscow nor Beijing has the final say. Give the corridor up, and someone else will take over. In the months ahead, this route will matter more. Maintaining a decades-old sanction against the country anchoring its western end does not read as cautious geopolitics in Baku. This reads as Washington being unsure of its goals.

Every president since George W. Bush has waived the sanction against Baku annually, including Trump. He extended the waiver again last August, citing counterterrorism and border-security needs. A statute the executive branch has neutered every year for more than two decades isn’t protecting anyone; it’s an insult that Azerbaijan has learned to live with — a legal loose end that Congress could tie off in a single vote.

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna’s (R-Fla.) bill , which has gathered co-sponsors and is now before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, would repeal the relevant section of the 1992 outright, citing Azerbaijan’s role as “a steadfast ally” and the border agreement already reached with Armenia. With Republican majorities in both chambers and an administration already on record waiving the provision, this is the most favorable environment for repeal since the law was written.

It simply requires Congress to admit that it no longer serves American interests to maintain a 1992 punishment for a conflict whose first phase ended in a 1994 ceasefire and whose military resolution came in 2020-2023, against a country now central to American energy security and an ongoing effort to counter Iran and Russia in the region.

Hollie McKay is a war correspondent and foreign policy analyst who has spent two decades reporting from conflict zones. She is the author of “Only Cry for the Living: Memos From Inside the ISIS Battlefield” and “Afghanistan: The End of the U.S. Footprint and the Rise of the Taliban Rule.”

articles.title: An 8,000-acre South Carolina forest was bought for conservation after drawing developer interest; the state now plans to acquire 4,148 acres for a new Carvers Bay State Forest
articles.summary: US News: A major land purchase in Georgetown County, South Carolina, is moving ahead as local officials support plans to turn 4,148 acres in Carvers Bay into a.
articles.body: A major land purchase in Georgetown County, South Carolina, is moving ahead as local officials support plans to turn 4,148 acres in Carvers Bay into a new state forest. According to a report by the Coastal Observer, the Georgetown County Board of Education voted to send formal letters of support to the South Carolina Forestry Commission for its planned purchase of the large tract on Eaddy Road, outside Dunbar Landing in the western part of the county. The 4,148-acre parcel is part of a larger 8,000-acre forest bought for $34.2 million by two nonprofit organisations, The Conservation Fund and the Malone Family Land Preservation Foundation. The property had attracted strong interest from commercial developers before the conservation groups stepped in to protect it. Under the proposed state plan, the remaining part of the 8,000-acre property along the Black River will become part of the Wildlife Management Area program run by the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources.Revenue sharing and public accessThe school board's support also has a direct financial connection to state forest operations. Under South Carolina law, the Forestry Commission gives 25 percent of the gross revenue from timber harvesting and state forest management to the local county. The money helps support public schools. School Board Member Eileen Johnson welcomed the proposed acquisition during the board meeting. She said development pressure in the southern part of the county is already limited by protected areas such as the Francis Marion National Forest. "We've got to preserve everything we can," Johnson said, according to the Coastal Observer. "I'm all about stewardship of our land." Johnson also said public recreational access would be an important part of the new Carvers Bay State Forest once the South Carolina Department of Administration completes the purchase.More protection on the Waccamaw NeckAlong with supporting the Carvers Bay project, the Georgetown County School Board also backed a separate conservation purchase involving the 3,492-acre Arcadia East tract on the Waccamaw Neck. Supporting the Arcadia East purchase means the school district will give up possible future tax income from a large residential and commercial development that Georgetown County originally approved in 2002. The long-term development plan allowed for 2,451 homes, a 500-room resort hotel and large amounts of office and commercial space. A county study from 2002 estimated that fully developing Arcadia East could have produced as much as $153.8 million in total tax revenue each year. The development would have made its residents and businesses the largest taxpayers in the county. However, the estimate did not include school taxes, which historically made up about two-thirds of local property tax bills. It also did not account for inflation or changing infrastructure costs. Last year, the Arcadia East property generated about $5,200 in combined county and school district taxes.Nonprofit support and fundingThe Department of Natural Resources plans to acquire Arcadia East with help from the South Carolina Office of Resilience and two nonprofit conservation organisations, the Open Space Institute and Ducks Unlimited. The nonprofit groups will hold the property title until all required state funding approvals are completed. The Georgetown County Council has also formally supported the Arcadia East deal, joining the school board in backing the purchase. "We're thrilled to have support from both the county and the school board," Emily Purcell, director of conservation programs for Ducks Unlimited, told the Coastal Observer. "We're excited to hopefully work towards a great conservation outcome in Georgetown County." The new effort builds on other conservation work in the area. In 2007, a permanent conservation easement was placed on 3,612 acres of the Arcadia West property west of U.S. Highway 17. Ducks Unlimited also holds and manages that easement. Responding to concerns about the possible loss of tax revenue from taking thousands of acres out of future development plans, Johnson said long-term land protection is more important than short-term tax income. "We've got plenty of land. I'm not worried about taxes right now," Johnson said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Americans in Middle East warned to ‘exercise heightened vigilance’ following strikes on Riyadh
articles.summary: The State Department on Saturday warned Americans in the Middle East to exercise caution, after the Iranian-backed Houthis launched an attack on the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh. Citing “tensions” in the region, the State Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs said the security environment in the Middle East “remains complex with the potential for unforeseen…
articles.body:
The State Department on Saturday warned Americans in the Middle East to exercise caution, after the Iranian-backed Houthis launched an attack on the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh.

Citing “tensions” in the region, the State Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs said the security environment in the Middle East “remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation.”

The bureau wrote on the social platform X , “Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” noting the Houthis’ attack on Riyadh.

The Houthis launched a ballistic missile toward the Saudi capital on Saturday, with some residents hearing an explosion and others seeing a plume of smoke near King Khalid International Airport, as reported by The Associated Press (AP).

The Houthis and Saudi Arabia have ramped up fighting in recent weeks, as the U.S.-Iran war approaches the seven-month mark.

Senior Houthi official Mohamed al-Bukhaiti told the AP on Sunday the Yemeni rebel group assured Trump administration officials it will not target American vessels in the Red Sea.

“We confirmed that we are not targeting the United States, or any other nation, in the strait, with the sole exception of the Saudi enemy,” al-Bukhaiti said.

President Trump considered joining Saudi Arabia in launching strikes against the Houthis over the weekend but decided against it Sunday, The New York Times reported.

The State Department’s consular affairs division noted Saturday the Houthi-Saudi conflict “has the potential to escalate rapidly” and urged Americans outside the Middle East to “seriously reconsider travel to and through” the region.

“Those who do travel to or from the region should monitor information about airport and airline operations. U.S. diplomatic facilities, including outside the Middle East, have been targeted,” the bureau added, noting the Islamic Republic and its proxy groups “may target other U.S. interests overseas.”

articles.title: Pakistan in crisis: PTI to hold Sept 27 stir 'at all costs'; Imran Khan's sisters challenge detention orders
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan's opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) will proceed with its planned September 27 protest demanding the release of jailed former prime m.
articles.body: Pakistan's opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) will proceed with its planned September 27 protest demanding the release of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, even as legal challenges have been filed against the preventive detention of his three sisters.A petition was filed in the Lahore High Court on Monday challenging the 30-day detention orders issued against Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, according to a report by Pakistan-based daily The Express Tribune, as cited by news agency ANI.The petition, filed by Shahraiz Khan, son of Aleema Khan, seeks to have the detention orders declared invalid and the immediate release of the three women.The detention orders were issued by the Lahore deputy commissioner on September 20 under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, ahead of PTI's planned September 27 demonstrations.Aleema Khan was detained earlier, while Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were detained on Monday.The petition alleged that Aleema Khan was intercepted while travelling for personal errands and that there was no public gathering or situation at the time that could pose a threat to public order. It also stated that Aleema Khan and her driver, Muhammad Ameer, were being held at Lahore Central Jail.The petitioner described Aleema Khan as a law-abiding individual and alleged that the detention order did not contain specific allegations justifying preventive detention.The respondents named in the petition include the home department secretary, Lahore deputy commissioner, capital city police officer and Lahore Central Jail superintendent, according to The Express Tribune.PTI says September 27 protest will go aheadKhyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi said on Monday that PTI would go ahead with its September 27 protest “at all costs”. He said the party would announce its detailed protest plan on September 25 and mobilise workers across Pakistan.Afridi said arrests of PTI provincial ministers and lawmakers had begun ahead of the protest, prompting an emergency meeting of the party's parliamentary group.He said the party had pursued “all constitutional and democratic avenues” but was being prevented from meeting Imran Khan despite court orders.Afridi said PTI had no intention of confrontation and would pursue its demands through peaceful and democratic means. He also said party workers would not carry weapons during the protest.PTI chairman Barrister Gohar said the party was not planning to “storm” Islamabad and would not take the law and order situation into its own hands. He said the authorities were provoking the party but PTI would not come to Islamabad “like terrorists”.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, meanwhile, said the government would not allow the September 27 protest to disrupt Islamabad. Speaking to reporters in Lahore on Monday, he said preparations were under way for an “assault” and that the government would not allow the capital to be shut down.Family condemns detentionsImran Khan's son, Kasim Khan, also condemned the detention of his relatives and appealed for international intervention.In a post on X, he said, “This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez, have now been abducted as well. They have broken into my aunties' and cousins' houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated.”He added, “No news has been released as to where they have been taken. This is criminal behaviour. Inexcusable. The Pakistani people are petrified of their own leaders. No upstanding nation should tolerate this criminal establishment. Intervention is now imperative. The world MUST take action.”The arrests come as PTI prepares for the September 27 protest seeking the release of Imran Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 and is currently held at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Former lawyer who pulled gun on ex-wife in Ohio restaurant is sentenced to nearly 25 years
articles.summary: A former lawyer who stormed into an Ohio restaurant and aimed a handgun at his ex-wife last April was sentenced to up to 24 ½ years in prison on Monday.
articles.body: A former lawyer who stormed into an Ohio restaurant and aimed a handgun at his ex-wife last April was sentenced to up to 24 ½ years in prison on Monday. Matthew Exton, 43, was convicted of two counts of attempted murder and two counts of felonious assault earlier this month in connection with the incident at a Toledo restaurant. Prosecutors said Exton tried to shoot his former spouse at close range with a Colt Defender as she sat at a table alongside her mother on April 11, 2025. Moments after the gun failed to go off because the weapon’s safety was on, a waiter and others tackled Exton and subdued him. Exton faced sentencing enhancements under Ohio law because of his use of a firearm while committing felonies. During his sentencing hearing Monday in Lucas County Common Pleas Court, prosecutors said a mass casualty event was avoided that day. “He nearly perpetrated a mass casualty event in the middle of a crowded restaurant. ... He had no regard for anyone or anything other than himself,” prosecutor Mike Loisel argued, according to a live feed of the proceedings. Loisel added that Exton is so unhinged that he “must be incarcerated” for a lengthy period of time. “This court has provided protection for all the victims in this matter and, quite honestly, to the public at large,” Loisel said. Exton, who divorced his wife in 2024, argued on his own behalf Monday after telling Judge Gary Cook he wanted to fire his lawyer. He insisted he did not intend to kill or harm his former spouse or her mother, even though surveillance video from the event played at his trial shows him charging at the pair with his gun drawn. In a series of arguments in court, in which he complained that he’s been treated unfairly, Exton insisted his charges were political and that he had no ill intentions. “Guns don’t kill people, people kill people. ... I didn’t kill anybody. I didn’t hurt any people, and I did not try,” Exton argued at his sentencing hearing. Judge Cook, however, debunked the defense by playing footage of the event before handing down a two-decade prison sentence. He pointed to a moment when Exton appears to scramble to unlock the safety lever after the weapon failed to fire. “You are flummoxed by the fact that it did not go off, and you’re trying to fix the safety,” Cook said. “That is the moment cementing your intent.”
