articles.title: Bessent says US, Chinese officials considering lowering tariffs on ‘noncritical’ items
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Monday officials from the U.S. and China are considering lowering tariffs on “noncritical” products, as President Trump prepares to host Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Washington, D.C. During an interview on CNBC’s “Squawk Box,” Bessent said the two sides “floated” a deal to reduce tariffs on $30 billion…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Monday officials from the U.S. and China are considering lowering tariffs on “noncritical” products, as President Trump prepares to host Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Washington, D.C.

During an interview on CNBC’s “ Squawk Box ,” Bessent said the two sides “floated” a deal to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods each country imports from the other during a May summit in Beijing.

Bessent added that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and his team met with Chinese officials for “most of the day” in New York City on Sunday and discussed such an agreement.

“They’ve been having extensive discussions before [on whether] there [are] items that are noncritical to both sides that we would like to take down to most favored nation tariff levels,” Bessent told host Joe Kernen, referencing trade advantages the U.S. and China would grant to each other that are greater than or equivalent to other parameters they provide to other countries.

Under the deal, American businesses would be able to export more agricultural goods and energy-related products to China, Bessent said.

Trump and Xi will meet in D.C. later this week, less than five months after the U.S. president met with his Chinese counterpart in Beijing. Trump left China without a deal to extend the trade truce that officials from the two countries agreed to last October.

That agreement, under which the president reduced tariffs on Chinese goods and Xi pledged to maintain export levels of critical minerals, expires on Nov. 10.

Greer said Monday on “ Bloomberg Surveillance ” the talks with Chinese officials in New York were “positive” and “constructive.”

But the U.S. trade representative accused China of limiting rare earth exports, noting it would be “naive” to say the two sides have “full trust and full confidence” in each other.

“That’s probably the right kind of range,” Greer said, when host Annmarie Hordern asked whether he backed a three- to six-month extension of the trade truce.

Amid the trade disputes with China during Trump’s second term, the U.S. trade deficit with Beijing fell last year to less than $202.7 billion, the lowest mark since 2005, according to data from the U.S. Census Bureau.

America’s trade deficit with China this year is on pace to be even lower, as it stood at roughly $91.2 billion as of the end of July, per the Census Bureau.

articles.title: Iran to attend UN assembly in New York — even as peace with US remains elusive
articles.summary: A slimmed-down Iranian delegation is due to touch down in New York on Tuesday for the United Nations General Assembly, as President Donald Trump touts the possibility of “very big things” ahead amid the war in the Middle East.
articles.body: A slimmed-down Iranian delegation is due to touch down in New York on Tuesday for the United Nations General Assembly, as President Donald Trump touts the possibility of “very big things” ahead amid the war in the Middle East. A founding member of the UN, Iran has maintained a presence at the global diplomatic event for decades, led most recently by the country’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and his predecessor, Ebrahim Raisi. But the presence of Iran’s delegation this year, on the home turf of a country with which it remains at war, is unprecedented in recent years. Which Iranian officials are allowed to attend? The Trump administration has said it will allow Iran’s “core delegation,” which will include Pezeshkian, to come to New York. This year’s delegation will be smaller than during the 2025 event, months before the US-Iran war started, a State Department spokesperson said Thursday. The exact makeup of Iran’s delegation is not yet known, but Iranian state media reported that Pezeshkian will travel to New York on Tuesday. “Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week,” the State Department spokesperson said. “The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our (sanctions) policy,” the official said. Section 11 of the UN Headquarters Agreement states that US authorities “shall not impose any impediments” on UN officials or representatives of member states to travel to or from the New York headquarters. Is the US-Iran war ongoing? No US strikes on Iran have been publicly reported for more than two weeks. Despite the lull, Trump indicated that major decisions on Iran may be approaching — a statement that risks aggravating tensions between the two nations ahead of the diplomatic gathering. Iran, meanwhile, has warned that any new US attack would trigger sustained strikes on US bases and interests across the region. Iran’s central military command said Sunday it had received information that the US, with the backing of some regional countries, ⁠is preparing to resume actions against ⁠Iran, the country’s semi-official Tasnim News Agency reported. Speaking to Fox News over the weekend, Trump said he was in “deciding mode” and that “very big things” could happen soon. He did not provide details. Has Iran attended before? Yes. Iran has attended the General Assembly in various forms for decades, through turbulent times as well as moments of diplomatic progress. Ayatollah Ali Khamenei addressed the assembly in 1987 when he was president, two years before he became supreme leader. Khamenei was killed in late February in an Israeli airstrike at the outset of the US-Israeli war with Iran. Notably, in 2015, Iran’s then-president, Hassan Rouhani, told world leaders that the landmark Iran nuclear deal signed that year — a focal point of President Barack Obama’s foreign policy — was a “victory over war” and should help bring peace to the Middle East. This year, though, the peace that Rouhani spoke of feels increasingly distant, with no sign of resumed negotiations between Washington and Tehran. The closest international equivalent to this year’s wartime meeting might be Egyptian President Anwar Sadat’s 1977 visit to Israel while the two countries were technically at war — but even that was part of a larger peace process. How will the visit work logistically? There are more questions than answers at this stage. The US has put restrictions on the Iranian delegation’s movements in the past. Last year, the Trump administration announced it was blocking Iranian diplomats from accessing the “wholesale club stores” like Costco and purchasing luxury goods while in the US. That policy remains in place, according to the State Department spokesperson. Iranian officials visiting New York for the UN General Assembly last year were also restricted “to the areas strictly necessary to transit to and from the UN headquarters district to conduct their official UN business.” In 2019, amid tensions between the two nations, the US imposed restrictions on the visiting delegation’s movements. Iran is not the only country to face obstacles over access. The Trump administration has again refused to issue a visa to Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. He is likely to address the chamber via video.

articles.title: Flights grounded at major US airports after construction workers cut backup cable
articles.summary: US News: Flights were disrupted across the US Northeast on Monday after a key air traffic control connection failed and a backup fiber optic cable was cut duri.
articles.body: Flights were disrupted across the US Northeast on Monday after a key air traffic control connection failed and a backup fiber optic cable was cut during construction work, forcing the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to temporarily halt some incoming flights at major airports including Newark Liberty, Philadelphia and Teterboro.The disruption was linked to communication problems at a Philadelphia air traffic control facility that handles traffic for several major airports in the region. The FAA said some incoming flights were temporarily halted because of the issues.FlightAware, a flight tracking website, said more than 300 flights at Newark and Philadelphia, or about 15%, had been delayed. Newark is a major hub for United Airlines, while Philadelphia is a hub for American Airlines.The technical problems also forced a number of flights to be diverted to other airports. Flightradar24 said flights at Newark were being delayed by an average of 112 minutes.Backup fiber cable cut during constructionFAA administrator Brian Bedford said a primary circuit at the Philadelphia air traffic control facility failed on Monday morning. The agency later discovered that a backup fiber optic line had been severed between New Brunswick and Newark, New Jersey.The FAA said it was working to restore the key connection by installing a new circuit on the primary line while also repairing the backup fiber optic cable.“That fiber break is probably 13 hours to repair. It’s massive,” Bedford said, according to a video posted online by a CBS transportation reporter.The primary circuit that failed is already scheduled to be replaced as part of a wider overhaul of the US air traffic control system.By early afternoon, some flights had begun to resume at LaGuardia and Philadelphia, but significant delays were expected to continue through the rest of Monday. Some airlines were also allowing passengers to change flights without paying fees.Previous disruptions at Philadelphia facilityThe latest disruption occurred at the same FAA facility that was linked to major flight disruptions at Newark Liberty International Airport in May 2025, when the facility suffered a series of communications outages.The FAA also said last year that a telecommunications outage at the Philadelphia facility had affected communications and radar displays used by air traffic controllers.The problems have renewed attention on the ageing US air traffic control infrastructure. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to address the system's ageing technology and increase the number of air traffic controllers, following years of complaints about congestion, flight delays and technical failures.The disruption also coincided with the FAA's launch of testing for a new computer system that uses artificial intelligence to predict scheduling conflicts and weather-related problems and help controllers reroute traffic.The AI system was initially being tested only in the Washington, D.C., area and did not appear to be connected to Monday's outages.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: For half a century, Massachusetts' Mill Brook ran beneath a downtown parking lot; Athol has now uncovered it, created 12,000 sq ft of wetlands and turned 53,000 sq ft of pavement into vegetation
articles.summary: US News: For decades, a stretch of Mill Brook in Athol, Massachusetts, was hidden beneath asphalt, largely out of sight beneath what had become a downtown park.
articles.body: For decades, a stretch of Mill Brook in Athol, Massachusetts, was hidden beneath asphalt, largely out of sight beneath what had become a downtown parking area. This month, the small central Massachusetts town celebrated a very different landscape: the stream is flowing in the open again, new wetlands surround it and much of the former pavement has been replaced with greenery. The transformation, known as Mill Brook Crossing, was officially completed with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on September 16. Reporting by Streetsblog Massachusetts and the Athol Daily News, along with information from the Massachusetts government, shows how the project turned a heavily paved commercial area into a greener public space designed to address flooding, extreme heat and pedestrian safety.A stream hidden beneath the pavementThe site was formerly known as Lord Pond Plaza, a large commercial area where Mill Brook had been confined underground in a culvert. The idea of bringing the stream back into the open emerged through Athol’s climate resilience planning. Massachusetts state documents say the project was designed to improve stream connectivity while addressing the area’s vulnerability to flooding and excessive heat. The town had identified the plaza as an urban heat island, with the large expanse of asphalt contributing to higher temperatures in the surrounding downtown area. The completed project has now daylighted approximately 500 linear feet of Mill Brook, allowing the perennial stream to run through the newly redesigned landscape rather than beneath the parking area.53,000 square feet of pavement gives way to vegetationOne of the most striking changes is the reduction in hard, impervious surfaces. About 53,000 square feet of pavement has been converted into vegetated areas, according to information presented by Athol officials at the project’s completion. The change allows more rainwater to infiltrate the ground instead of rapidly running across asphalt and entering drainage systems.The project also created approximately 12,000 square feet of new wetlands, alongside habitat for pollinators and wildlife. More than 80 trees were planted, expanding the downtown tree canopy and helping address the urban heat island effect.Designed to manage stormwater naturallyMill Brook Crossing is not simply a landscaping project. Much of its design is based on using natural systems to manage some of the problems created by extensive pavement. The redesigned area incorporates rain gardens, bioswales and porous pavement, which can help slow and capture stormwater while reducing runoff and supporting better water quality. The Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs has highlighted the project as an example of using stream restoration and green infrastructure to address both flooding and heat. That approach is particularly relevant in a location where the stream had previously been confined beneath a developed area.The parking lot was also a safety concernThe former plaza presented another problem beyond its environmental impact. The large, open parking area had complicated vehicle and pedestrian movement, with town planning documents previously identifying concerns around traffic circulation and pedestrian safety.The redesigned space introduces a more organised layout along with new sidewalks and pedestrian infrastructure. Massachusetts’ Complete Streets program provided nearly $250,000 for sidewalk improvements connected with the project.A project years in the makingThe transformation did not happen overnight. Athol began exploring the redevelopment through its Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness planning in 2020. The town subsequently received state funding for engineering and design before securing construction funding.The broader redevelopment ultimately became a roughly $3 million construction project, with additional support for related pedestrian improvements. In July 2026, Athol’s Select Board formally changed the site’s name from Lord Pond Plaza to Mill Brook Crossing, reflecting the restored stream and the area’s new identity.From parking space to climate-resilient public spaceWhat once largely functioned as a sea of asphalt is now a landscape built around a visible stream, wetlands, trees and other green infrastructure. For Athol, the project represents a shift in how a downtown space can be used: rather than treating the buried waterway and surrounding pavement simply as infrastructure, the town has brought part of the natural landscape back into view while creating a public area intended to better handle heat and stormwater. The result is a downtown setting where a stream that spent decades underground once again forms part of the town’s visible landscape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Americans rate UN poorly in five key areas: Survey
articles.summary: A new poll shows that many Americans have a poor outlook on the United Nations and its performance in five chief objectives. The Gallup poll released Sunday found that 73 percent were most critical of the U.N.’s efforts to uphold international peace and security, with 25 percent saying the international body is doing a good…
articles.body:
A new poll shows that many Americans have a poor outlook on the United Nations and its performance in five chief objectives.

The Gallup poll released Sunday found that 73 percent were most critical of the U.N.’s efforts to uphold international peace and security, with 25 percent saying the international body is doing a good job. Seventy percent rated the U.N. poorly on both upholding international law and protecting human rights, and 28 percent say the U.N. has done well with both objectives.

Sixty-three percent say the U.N. has done poorly in supporting sustainable development, compared to 34 percent who say the U.N. is doing a good job.

Over half of Americans also rated the U.N.’s ability to deliver humanitarian assistance such as food, shelter and medical care to people affected by war, famine or natural disasters poorly, at 53 percent. Forty-five percent rate the U.N.’s assistance to people affected by war, famine or other disasters favorably.

Gallup stated that these negative ratings are consistent with Americans’ recent evaluations of the U.N.’s overall job performance, finding that about six in 10 view it as doing a poor job in handling world problems.

Pollsters did find that Americans still have a positive outlook on the U.N. as an organization and its missions. These opinions are split by partisanship, with 55 percent of Democrats rating the U.N. as best on humanitarian assistance, followed by 43 percent of independents and 36 percent of Republicans.

Democrats lead in favoring the U.N.’s support for sustainable development at 44 percent, and 32 percent of independents and 27 percent of Republicans feel the same. The U.N.’s ability to protect human rights is favored by 33 percent of Democrats, 25 percent of independents and 27 percent of Republicans.

The U.N.’s objective to uphold international law received similar support. Thirty-five percent of Democrats, 26 percent of independents and 25 percent of Republicans approve of the international body’s handling of this issue.

Democrats, independents and Republicans’ lowest approval rating goes toward the U.N.’s objective to maintain international peace and security, at 32 percent, 23 percent and 19 percent, respectively.

“As has been the case for most of the past two decades, Americans support the United Nations as an institution but don’t think it is doing an effective job of handling the problems it has faced,” pollsters wrote. “The last time a majority of Americans approved of the job the UN was doing was in the period after 9/11.”

Gallup noted that the poll’s release comes ahead of the annual U.N. General Assembly this week, and as the international community faces several challenges, including the Russian-Ukrainian war, Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran.

Americans’ views toward the U.N. differ from those of other countries. Gallup released a separate poll showing that majorities in 67 countries approve of the organization’s job performance, with nine countries disapproving of the U.N.’s handling of issues.

The Gallup survey on how Americans grade the U.N. was conducted Sept. 1-14 and included 2,024 respondents. The margin of error is 4 percentage points.
